name: Anomalocaris canadensis
dietDetails: Preyed upon soft-bodied marine organisms, trilobites, and other Cambrian animals.
discoveryHistory: First discovered in the Burgess Shale of British Columbia by Joseph Whiteaves in 1892. Parts of its body were initially mistaken for three separate creatures (shrimp-like appendages, jellyfish-like mouth cone, and sponge-like torso).
interestingFacts: Considered one of the earliest apex predators in Earth's history.
Had highly advanced compound eyes with up to 16,000 lenses, providing keen vision in Cambrian seas.
Propelled itself through the water by undulating flexible lobes along the sides of its body.
sizeNotes: Estimated at 1 to 2 kg body mass; length excludes tail filaments.

name: Hallucigenia sparsa
dietDetails: Likely fed on organic detritus, sponges, or small animals on the seafloor.
discoveryHistory: First described by Charles Walcott in 1911 as a worm. Simon Conway Morris redescribed it in 1977, reconstructuring it upside down and backward, mistaking its tentacles for legs and its spines for support struts.
interestingFacts: For decades, paleontologists argued about which end was the head and which was the tail.
It had 7 pairs of long, rigid spines on its back and 7 pairs of delicate, clawed tentacles on its underside.
It is now recognized as a relative of modern velvet worms (Onychophorans).
sizeNotes: Extremely small, ranging from 0.5 to 5.5 cm in length.

name: Opabinia regalis
nameMeaning: Named after Opabin Pass, British Columbia
dietDetails: Soft-bodied bottom dwellers and organic debris.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Charles Walcott in 1912 in the Burgess Shale. Harry Whittington redescribed it in 1975, and its bizarre features initially drew laughter at a scientific conference.
interestingFacts: Possessed five stalked eyes that likely provided a 360-degree field of view.
Had a long, flexible nozzle-like snout (proboscis) with a clawed tip, used to grab food and transfer it to its backward-facing mouth.
It had 15 segments with lobed gills along its sides, but lacked legs.
sizeNotes: Typically 4 to 7 cm in length, excluding the proboscis.

name: Dunkleosteus terrelli
dietDetails: Fish, sharks, and even smaller Dunkleosteus individuals (cannibalism).
discoveryHistory: First discovered in 1867 by Jay Terrell in Ohio. Named Dunkleosteus in 1956 to honor David Dunkle, curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Cleveland Museum.
interestingFacts: Instead of teeth, it had massive, self-sharpening bony plates (gnathal plates) that acted like shears.
Could open its mouth in one-fiftieth of a second, creating a powerful vacuum to suck in prey.
Its bite force is estimated to have been around 6,000 to 7,400 Newtons at the tip of the blade.
sizeNotes: Recent studies suggest length estimates might be shorter (around 4.1 meters) due to placoderm body ratios.

name: Tiktaalik roseae
dietDetails: Small fish and invertebrates in shallow freshwater streams.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada, by a team led by Edward Daeschler, Neil Shubin, and Farish Jenkins.
interestingFacts: Represents a key evolutionary transition (a 'fishapod') between lobe-finned fish and early tetrapods.
Had a flat head and eyes on top, similar to a crocodile, and a flexible neck (unlike fish, which have fused neck bones).
Its wrist bones and primitive ribs were strong enough to support its body weight in shallow water or on land.
sizeNotes: Ranged from 1.25 to 2.75 meters (4 to 9 feet) in length.

name: Ichthyostega stensioei
nameMeaning: Fish roof (referring to the skull structure)
dietDetails: Fish and large invertebrates found in swampy river deltas.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in East Greenland by Lauge Koch's expedition in 1929. Described by Gunnar Säve-Söderbergh in 1932.
interestingFacts: One of the first Devonian tetrapods discovered and described.
Had seven toes on its hind feet rather than the standard five, showing early tetrapods experimented with digit numbers.
Probably moved on land like a mudskipper or elephant seal, pulling itself forward with its forelimbs.
sizeNotes: Estimated length of 1.5 meters (5 feet). Highly robust body skeleton.

name: Arthropleura armata
dietDetails: Decaying vegetation, spores, and lycopsid leaf litter in carboniferous rainforests.
discoveryHistory: First described in 1854 by Jordan and von Meyer based on partial fossils in Germany. A massive, near-complete fossil was found in Northumberland, England in 2018.
interestingFacts: The largest known terrestrial invertebrate of all time.
Grew to its massive size due to high atmospheric oxygen levels (up to 35%) and a lack of large vertebrate predators.
Had between 30 and 60 body segments and dozens of jointed legs.
sizeNotes: Ranged from 0.3 to 2.6 meters long; estimated weight up to 50 kg.

name: Meganeura monyi
dietDetails: Other flying insects, small amphibians, and early reptiles.
discoveryHistory: Found in Commentry, France, in 1880. Described by French paleontologist Charles Brongniart in 1885.
interestingFacts: Often described as a giant prehistoric dragonfly, though it belongs to a distinct related group (griffinflies).
Wingspan reached up to 70 centimeters, making it one of the largest known flying insect species.
Like modern dragonflies, it likely had huge compound eyes and hunted primarily by sight.
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 65 to 71 cm; body length: ~43 cm. Weight estimates range from 100 to 200 grams.

name: Dimetrodon grandis
dietDetails: Fish, amphibians, and other reptiles like Eryops and Edaphosaurus.
discoveryHistory: First named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1878. Numerous skeletons have been discovered in the Red Beds of Texas.
interestingFacts: Often mistaken for a dinosaur, but it is actually a synapsid (a stem-mammal), making it more closely related to humans than to dinosaurs.
The massive sail on its back was formed by elongated neural spines and likely used for thermoregulation or display.
It had two distinct types of teeth (shearing and stabbing), a feature not seen in reptiles.
sizeNotes: Ranged from 1.7 to 4.6 meters long across various species; D. grandis was one of the largest.

name: Edaphosaurus pogonias
dietDetails: Tough terrestrial plants, horsetails, and ferns, crushed with its specialized tooth plates.
discoveryHistory: Described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1882 from Texas. It was one of the earliest known dominant land herbivores.
interestingFacts: Like Dimetrodon, it possessed a large sail, but its sail had horizontal crossbars resembling crossbeams.
Had tooth plates on the roof of its mouth and inner jaws, forming a grinding battery to crush vegetation.
It had a remarkably small skull relative to its massive, barrel-shaped body.
sizeNotes: Ranged from 1 to 3.5 meters in length. Weight reached up to 300 kg.

name: Helicoprion bessonowi
dietDetails: Soft-bodied cephalopods like ammonites and belemnites.
discoveryHistory: First described by Alexander Karpinsky in 1899 from fossils found in the Ural Mountains. For over a century, the position of the 'tooth whorl' was debated.
interestingFacts: The tooth whorl was located inside the lower jaw, acting like a circular saw blade to slice soft prey.
It is a stem-ratfish, closer to modern chimaeras than to modern sharks.
As new teeth grew, the older teeth were pushed inward, creating the spiral whorl rather than shedding.
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 5 to 8 meters (16 to 26 feet) based on tooth whorl proportions.

name: Scutosaurus karpinskii
dietDetails: Low-lying plants, shrubs, and roots in dry, arid environments.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the Sokolki assembly on the Northern Dvina River in Russia by Vladimir Amalitsky. Described posthumously in 1921.
interestingFacts: Its skin was covered in bony plates (osteoderms) that acted as heavy armor against predators.
Its limbs were positioned directly beneath its body, a relatively advanced feature for Permian reptiles.
Likely had a large, complex digestive tract to break down fibrous plant material.
sizeNotes: Grew up to 3 meters (10 feet) long, weighing around 1 metric ton.

name: Inostrancevia alexandri
nameMeaning: Named after Russian geologist Aleksandr Inostrantsev
dietDetails: Large herbivores like Scutosaurus and dicynodonts.
discoveryHistory: First fossils found by Vladimir Amalitsky in northern Russia in the late 1890s. Described in 1922.
interestingFacts: The largest known gorgonopsian, a group of saber-toothed mammal-like synapsids.
Possessed enormous, flattened saber canines up to 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) long.
Fossils of a related species were discovered in South Africa in 2023, showing the genus migrated across continents.
sizeNotes: Total length reached up to 3.5 meters (11.5 feet), with a skull length of 50 cm.

name: Coelophysis bauri
dietDetails: Insects, small reptiles, fish, and early mammals.
discoveryHistory: First discovered by David Baldwin in 1881 in New Mexico. Described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1889. Thousands of complete skeletons were found at Ghost Ranch, NM, in 1947.
interestingFacts: One of the earliest known dinosaurs, exhibiting a highly successful, agile body plan.
Early claims of cannibalism (based on baby bones inside rib cages) were later disproved; the bones belonged to small crocodylomorphs.
Its bones were hollow and thin-walled, similar to those of modern birds.
sizeNotes: Slender build, typical specimens were 2 to 3 meters long and weighed around 15 to 25 kg.

name: Plateosaurus trossingensis
dietDetails: High foliage, cycads, and conifers, processed with leaf-shaped teeth.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1834 near Nuremberg, Germany, by Johann Engelhardt. Described by Hermann von Meyer in 1837.
interestingFacts: An early sauropodomorph, a group that would eventually evolve into the giant, long-necked sauropods.
Strictly bipedal; its hands were unable to rotate, making quadrupedal walking anatomically impossible.
Fossil mass graves in Europe suggest they traveled in herds or became trapped in mud flats.
sizeNotes: Highly variable adult sizes, ranging from 4.8 to 10 meters in length and 600 to 4,000 kg.

name: Postosuchus kirkpatricki
dietDetails: Small dinosaurs, dicynodonts, and other armored reptiles.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Garza County, Texas, by Sankar Chatterjee in 1980. Named in 1985 after the Kirkpatrick family, who owned the ranch where the fossils were found.
interestingFacts: Not a dinosaur, but a rauisuchian (an archosaur closer to crocodiles) that was the apex predator of Triassic North America.
Walked primarily on two legs (bipedal) based on limb proportions, though older reconstructions showed it on all fours.
Had a deep, powerful skull containing long, serrated dagger-like teeth.
sizeNotes: Ranged from 3.5 to 4 meters in length, with weight estimated up to 300 kg.

media.credit: Petrified Forest from Petrified Forest, USA (Public domain)

name: Dilophosaurus wetherilli
dietDetails: Preyed upon fish, small dinosaurs, and early herbivorous reptiles.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Northern Arizona by Jesse Williams in 1942. Named Dilophosaurus in 1970 by Samuel Paul Welles.
interestingFacts: Made famous by Jurassic Park, but the real animal was much larger, did not spit venom, and lacked a neck frill.
The twin crests on its skull were paper-thin and likely used for species recognition and courtship displays.
Its jaw was loosely connected near the front, which may have allowed it to catch fish or hook prey.
sizeNotes: Grew up to 6 meters (20 feet) long, weighing about 400 kg.

name: Stegosaurus stenops
nameMeaning: Roof lizard with a narrow face
dietDetails: Low-lying plants, mosses, ferns, horsetails, and cycads.
discoveryHistory: First found in Colorado in 1877 by M.P. Felch. Described by Othniel Charles Marsh during the famous Bone Wars.
interestingFacts: Had 17 flat bony plates on its back that were not used for armor but likely for display or temperature regulation.
Its tail weapon, consisting of 4 long spikes, is formally called a 'thagomizer' (a term coined in a Far Side cartoon).
Its brain was famously tiny, about the size of a walnut, weighing only 80 grams.
sizeNotes: Large individuals reached up to 9 meters in length and up to 7 metric tons.

name: Brachiosaurus altithorax
nameMeaning: Arm lizard with a deep chest
dietDetails: High canopy conifers, ginkgos, and tree ferns.
discoveryHistory: First discovered in the Grand River Valley, Colorado, by Elmer Riggs in 1900. Described in 1903.
interestingFacts: Its front legs were longer than its hind legs, giving its back a sloping profile similar to a giraffe.
Unlike other sauropods, it held its neck nearly vertically to reach high-altitude vegetation.
Had massive, chisel-like teeth to crop leaves from tall branches without chewing them.
sizeNotes: Length estimates range from 18 to 22 meters; weight ranges from 28 to 58 metric tons.

name: Allosaurus fragilis
dietDetails: Medium to large herbivorous dinosaurs like Stegosaurus and sauropods.
discoveryHistory: First described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877 based on fragmentary remains from Colorado. Dozens of individuals were later found at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
interestingFacts: The most common large predator of Late Jurassic North America, accounting for a vast majority of theropod fossils found.
Its skull was highly flexible and could expand laterally, allowing it to swallow large chunks of meat.
Had a lower bite force than modern lions, suggesting it used its skull like an axe to slash at prey.
sizeNotes: Average length was 8.5 meters (28 feet), but rare large specimens (like Saurophaganax) reached 11-12 meters.

name: Archaeopteryx lithographica
nameMeaning: Ancient wing from the lithographic limestone
dietDetails: Insects, small lizards, and early mammals.
discoveryHistory: First fossil (a single feather) discovered in 1860 in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany. The famous London Specimen was found in 1861.
interestingFacts: Famous transitional fossil representing the link between non-avian theropod dinosaurs and modern birds.
Had flight feathers like a bird, but retained reptilian features: a long bony tail, three clawed fingers, and a jaw with teeth.
Its discovery occurred just two years after Charles Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species', serving as key evidence.
sizeNotes: Roughly the size of a modern common raven or magpie, weighing 0.5 to 1.0 kg.

name: Yi qi
dietDetails: Small vertebrates, insects, and soft plant matter in forest canopies.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by a farmer in Hebei Province, China. Described in 2015 by Xu Xing and colleagues.
interestingFacts: Had bat-like wings made of a membranous skin stretched between long fingers and a unique bony rod (styliform element).
One of the smallest known non-avian dinosaurs, adapting to an arboreal, gliding lifestyle.
Its plumage preserved melanosomes, suggesting it had black and brown coloration.
sizeNotes: Wingspan was around 60 cm; weighed roughly 380 grams.

name: Spinosaurus aegyptiacus
dietDetails: Large fish (e.g. Mawsonia), sharks, sawfish, and occasionally land animals.
discoveryHistory: First described by Ernst Stromer in 1915 from Egyptian fossils. Those holotype fossils were destroyed in a Munich bombing raid during WWII. New specimens were described in 2014.
interestingFacts: The longest known carnivorous dinosaur, exceeding even Tyrannosaurus rex in length.
Adapted for a semi-aquatic lifestyle, featuring dense bones for buoyancy, a paddle-like tail, and nostrils located high on its snout.
The massive sail on its back was formed by neural spines up to 1.65 meters long.
sizeNotes: Length estimates range from 14 to 15.6 meters; weight ranges from 6.4 to 8.7 metric tons.

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large herbivores like Triceratops and Edmontosaurus.
discoveryHistory: First discovered by Arthur Lakes in Colorado (1874), later named and described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905.
interestingFacts: Had one of the strongest bite forces among all terrestrial animals, estimated at 35,000 to 57,000 Newtons.
Its tiny two-clawed arms were surprisingly strong, capable of lifting around 200 kilograms each.
Whether it had feathers is still debated, though direct fossil impressions show predominantly scaly skin.
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 8,400 to 14,000 kg depending on study.

name: Triceratops horridus
dietDetails: Low-growing vegetation like ferns, cycads, and palms, cropped with its powerful beak.
discoveryHistory: First found near Denver, Colorado, in 1887 by George Lyman Cannon. Described by Othniel Charles Marsh.
interestingFacts: The large frill and three horns were likely used for defense against predators and in courtship or dominance displays.
Its skull was one of the largest of any land animal, reaching up to 2.5 meters in length.
Lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex, and fossil bones show healed T. rex bite marks, proving they clashed.
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 6,000 to 12,000 kg depending on body mass calculations.

name: Velociraptor mongoliensis
dietDetails: Small dinosaurs, reptiles, and mammals; famous for preying on Protoceratops.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia in 1923 by Peter Kaisen. Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1924.
interestingFacts: In reality, it was about the size of a turkey, and was fully covered in feathers (quill knobs were found on its forearm bones).
Possessed a large, curved sickle claw on each second toe, which it likely used to pin down and puncture prey.
A famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil preserves a Velociraptor locked in combat with a Protoceratops, buried instantly by a collapsing sand dune.
sizeNotes: About 2 meters long, 0.5 meters high at the hip. Weighed around 15 kg.

name: Parasaurolophus walkeri
dietDetails: High and low vegetation, conifers, leaves, and twigs, processed with grinding dental batteries.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Alberta, Canada, in 1920 by William Parks. Described in 1922.
interestingFacts: The hollow, curved crest on its head functioned as a resonating chamber to produce low-frequency vocalizations.
Could walk on both two legs (when running or browsing) and four legs (when slow walking or grazing).
Its crest was also likely used for visual display and species identification.
sizeNotes: Grew to about 9.5 meters long; weight estimated at 2.5 metric tons.

name: Ankylosaurus magniventris
nameMeaning: Fused lizard with a great belly
dietDetails: Low-growing plants, ferns, and shrubs, cropped with its broad beak.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana by Barnum Brown in 1906. Described in 1908.
interestingFacts: Had a heavy armor of bony osteoderms and a massive bony club at the end of its tail, used for self-defense.
The tail club was supported by fused vertebrae, allowing it to deliver bone-shattering blows to attackers.
Lived in the same environments as Tyrannosaurus rex, serving as one of its most heavily fortified prey.
sizeNotes: Ranged from 6 to 8 meters long; weighed roughly 5 to 8 metric tons.

name: Carnotaurus sastrei
dietDetails: Medium-sized herbivores and small dinosaurs in open dry landscapes.
discoveryHistory: Found in Chubut Province, Argentina, by Anselmo Sastre in 1984 during an expedition led by José Bonaparte.
interestingFacts: Possessed two distinct, thick horns above its eyes, unique among carnivorous dinosaurs.
Its forelimbs were vestigial, even smaller than those of T. rex, and lacked claws entirely.
Had extremely fast leg muscles, making it one of the fastest running large theropods known.
sizeNotes: Ranged from 7.5 to 9 meters in length; weight is estimated around 1.35 metric tons.

media.credit: Lida Xing and Yi Liu (CC BY 2.5)

name: Quetzalcoatlus northropi
nameMeaning: Named after the Aztec feathered serpent god Quetzalcoatl
dietDetails: Small vertebrates, carrion, and terrestrial prey.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Big Bend National Park, Texas, by Douglas A. Lawson in 1971. Described in 1975.
interestingFacts: The largest known flying animal in Earth's history, with a wingspan comparable to a small private airplane.
When standing on the ground, it was as tall as a modern giraffe (around 5.5 meters).
Likely hunted on land by stalking prey on all fours, similar to modern marabou storks.
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 10 to 11 meters; weight estimates range from 70 to 250 kg due to light, air-filled bones.

name: Pteranodon longiceps
dietDetails: Fishes, squids, and small marine organisms caught by diving.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1870 in the Smoky Hill Chalk of Kansas. It was the first pterosaur found outside Europe.
interestingFacts: Unlike earlier pterosaurs, it lacked teeth and had a bird-like beak.
Males had a large, backward-pointing crest on their skull, likely used for display and steering.
Fossils suggest they spent most of their time gliding over the Western Interior Seaway.
sizeNotes: Wingspan: 5.6 meters for females, up to 7.2 meters for males. Weight: ~30 to 90 kg.

name: Mosasaurus hoffmannii
dietDetails: Fish, ammonites, sharks, plesiosaurs, sea turtles, and even smaller mosasaurs.
discoveryHistory: First found in a chalk quarry near Maastricht, Netherlands, in 1764. The skull became famous when French revolutionary forces confiscated it in 1794.
interestingFacts: Not a dinosaur, but a giant marine reptile closely related to modern monitor lizards and snakes.
Had a second row of teeth (pterygoid teeth) on the roof of its mouth, preventing prey from escaping down its throat.
Propelled itself through water with a powerful, shark-like tail fin, using its flippers only for steering.
sizeNotes: Large specimens reached up to 15 to 17 meters in length; weight is estimated at 10 to 15 metric tons.

name: Elasmosaurus platyurus
nameMeaning: Thin-plate lizard with a flat tail
dietDetails: Small bony fish, squids, and shelled cephalopods.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in Kansas in 1867 by Theophilus Turner. Described by Edward Drinker Cope, who notoriously reconstructed the fossil with the head on the tail end.
interestingFacts: Had an extremely long neck consisting of 72 neck vertebrae, more than any other known animal.
Its neck was relatively rigid and could not be bent like a snake; it likely swam slowly beneath fish schools and darted its head up.
Swallowed small pebbles (gastroliths) to help grind food and control its buoyancy.
sizeNotes: Total length was 10.3 meters (34 feet), of which 7.1 meters was the neck.

name: Gastornis parisiensis
dietDetails: Tough plant material, nuts, seeds, and fruit, crushed using its massive bill.
discoveryHistory: First discovered near Paris in 1855 by Gaston Planté. For over a century, it was known under the synonym Diatryma in North America.
interestingFacts: For a long time, it was reconstructed as a terrifying carnivore preying on early horses, but chemical analysis of calcium isotopes in its bones proved it was a herbivore.
It was a flightless bird with tiny vestigial wings but possessed massive, muscular legs.
Its beak was extremely deep and strong, designed to crack open hard shells and seeds.
sizeNotes: Grew up to 2 meters (6.6 feet) tall; weight ranged from 150 to 200 kg.

name: Basilosaurus cetoides
nameMeaning: King lizard (named before its whale nature was known)
dietDetails: Fish, sharks, and smaller marine mammals like Dorudon.
discoveryHistory: Fossils were common in the southeastern US, where they were used as fireplace irons. Richard Harlan described it as a reptile in 1834, but Richard Owen identified it as a whale in 1839.
interestingFacts: One of the earliest fully aquatic whales, though it looked more like a giant sea serpent.
Retained tiny, vestigial hind limbs with feet and toes, a remnant of its land-dwelling ancestors.
Its jaw had teeth of different shapes (heterodonty), allowing it to grasp and slice prey.
sizeNotes: Elongated body shape. Length: 15 to 20 meters. Weight: ~5 to 7 metric tons.

name: Megalodon
dietDetails: Large marine mammals, baleen whales, seals, sirenians, and sea turtles.
taxonomicClassification: Chondrichthyes -> Lamniformes -> Otodontidae -> Otodus -> O. megalodon
discoveryHistory: Fossil teeth were historically regarded as petrified tongues of dragons. Nicolas Steno identified them as shark teeth in 1667. Named Otodus megalodon in 1843.
interestingFacts: The largest predatory shark to have ever lived, with teeth reaching up to 18 centimeters (7 inches) in length.
Its skeleton was made of cartilage, which rarely fossilizes, leaving only teeth and rare vertebrae for study.
Extinction was likely driven by global cooling and competition with ancestors of the great white shark and killer whale.
sizeNotes: Estimates range from 15 to 20 meters (50 to 65 feet); weight estimates range from 30 to 65 metric tons.

name: Smilodon fatalis
dietDetails: Large herbivores like bison, camels, horses, and ground sloths.
discoveryHistory: First described by Joseph Leidy in 1869 from Texas. Over 3,500 individual skeletons have been recovered from the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles.
interestingFacts: The most famous 'saber-toothed cat', possessing canine teeth up to 18 centimeters (7 inches) long.
Much more robustly built than modern big cats, with extremely powerful forelimbs used to pin down prey.
Its jaw could open to a wide 120-degree angle, but its bite force was weaker than that of a modern lion.
sizeNotes: Length: 1.75 meters (excluding short tail); height: 1.0 meter at shoulder. Weight: 160 to 280 kg.

name: Mammuthus primigenius
dietDetails: Grasses, sedges, shrubs, and herbaceous plants in the mammoth steppe.
discoveryHistory: First scientifically described by Johann Friedrich Blumenbach in 1799. Mummified remains with intact skin, hair, and muscle have been found in Siberian permafrost.
interestingFacts: Coexisted with early humans, who hunted them and depicted them in cave paintings (e.g. Rouffignac Cave, France).
Had a thick double coat of brown hair, small ears, and a short tail to minimize heat loss in freezing climates.
Its massive, curved tusks could grow up to 4.2 meters long and were likely used to shovel snow off vegetation.
sizeNotes: Males stood 2.7 to 3.4 meters tall at the shoulder; females were smaller. Weight: 4 to 6 metric tons.

name: Megatherium americanum
dietDetails: Leaves, twigs, and shrubs; could stand on hind legs to reach high branches.
discoveryHistory: First fossil discovered in 1788 on the banks of the Luján River in Argentina by Manuel Torres. Described by Georges Cuvier in 1796.
interestingFacts: One of the largest land mammals to have ever lived, comparable in size and weight to modern elephants.
Possessed enormous claws on its hands, likely used to pull down tree branches and strip them of foliage.
Capable of standing and walking bipedally on its hind legs to browse high vegetation.
sizeNotes: Total length reached up to 6 meters (20 feet) from head to tail; weighed around 4 metric tons.

name: Coelodonta antiquitatis
dietDetails: Grasses, sedges, and woody tundra vegetation.
discoveryHistory: First described in 1799 by Johann Friedrich Blumenbach. Well-preserved specimens have been found frozen in Siberia and oil-soaked in Poland.
interestingFacts: Possessed a massive, flat horn up to 1.3 meters long, which it used to sweep snow away to find plants.
Covered in thick, shaggy reddish-brown hair to withstand the freezing temperatures of Ice Age Europe.
Frequently depicted in Palaeolithic cave art alongside woolly mammoths.
sizeNotes: Grew up to 3.8 meters (12 feet) in length; stood 2.0 meters tall. Weight: ~1.8 to 2.7 metric tons.

name: Doedicurus clavicaudatus
nameMeaning: Pestle tail (referring to the tail club)
dietDetails: Low-growing grasses, herbs, and wetland plants.
discoveryHistory: Described in 1874 by Richard Owen from fossils found in Argentina. It was one of the largest glyptodonts.
interestingFacts: A giant prehistoric relative of armadillos with a huge, dome-shaped carapace made of fused bony studs.
The end of its tail featured a large, spiked bony club that resembled a medieval morning star.
Its armor was so solid that early human settlers in South America reportedly used the shells as shelters.
sizeNotes: Total length was 4.0 meters; shell height was 1.5 meters. Weighed about 1.4 metric tons.

name: Thylacoleo carnifex
dietDetails: Large marsupials like Diprotodon and giant kangaroos.
discoveryHistory: First described by Richard Owen in 1859 from fossil fragments. A near-complete skeleton was discovered in Flight Star Cave, Western Australia in 2002.
interestingFacts: The largest carnivorous mammal known to have lived in Australia.
Possessed enormous, bolt-cutter-like premolar teeth that could easily crush bone and slice flesh.
Had retractable claws, including a huge semi-opposable thumb claw used to grasp and dispatch prey.
sizeNotes: Stood 75 cm at shoulder; length 1.5 meters. Weighed 90 to 130 kg, comparable to a small female lion.

media.credit: Original uploader was roman uchytel, Rom-diz at Russian Wikipedia (Public domain)

name: Diprotodon optatum
dietDetails: Shrubs, twigs, leaves, and saltbush in dry, open woodlands.
discoveryHistory: First found in the early 1830s in Wellington Caves, New South Wales. Described by Richard Owen in 1838.
interestingFacts: The largest known marsupial of all time, standing as tall as a modern rhinoceros.
Related to modern wombats and koalas, featuring a backward-facing pouch to prevent dirt entry while digging.
Fossil footprints show they traveled in herds, migrating across Australia's interior to find water.
sizeNotes: Length: ~3.8 meters; height at shoulder: 2.0 meters. Weighed up to 2.8 metric tons.
